docs.title: Amendment: continuous fixed quality (2026-09-11; superseded for built-in defaults below)
docs.text:
Fixed(qualityFraction) now interpolates the total input pixel fraction between the supported minimum and full resolution, replacing the three-bucket fixed selector above. The minimum is an internal implementation value, not a documented numeric guarantee. Interpolation is linear in total input pixels, rather than each dimension. The public name and finite 0f..1f validation remain unchanged. Renderer resource limits and whole-pixel rounding still apply.

Quality = Fixed(1f) and Performance = Fixed(0f) retain their previous scales. Balanced = Fixed(0.5f) requests the midpoint between minimum and full-resolution pixel counts. Adaptive retains its previous scales, workload thresholds, cadence handling, and hysteresis; its tiers are resolved independently from fixed quality.

The implementation preserves the existing minimum fixed resolution. It is not a newly measured visual quality threshold. Fresh paired visual and performance testing remains necessary before changing Adaptive's default behavior. Earlier benchmark tables describe the old fixed profiles and must not be interpreted as measurements of this new mapping.

docs.title: Amendment: fixed built-in defaults (2026-09-24)
docs.text:
Built-in Blur and Glass now use the fixed Balanced profile through HazePerformanceMode.Default. HazePerformanceMode.Adaptive remains deprecated for binary compatibility and resolves exactly like Default. The cadence, workload thresholds, hysteresis, and adaptive tiers described above have been removed from built-in production rendering. HazeInputUpdateCadence has also been removed. HazeSampling.Adaptive remains unchanged for custom effects.

The prior built-in adaptive policy could not be supported as a technically reliable cross-effect contract. The public compatibility object therefore no longer promises adaptation. ADR-0004 and ADR-0005 remain the historical rationale and evidence for the removed policies. Their captured measurements and the earlier benchmark tables are preserved as history; active benchmark scenarios and current guidance cover fixed modes only. This change does not add new physical-device benchmark evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Issue #1206: Calibrate performance modes
  • ADR-0004: Use quality-gated adaptive input scaling for blur
  • ADR-0005: Use cadence-weighted adaptive input scaling for Glass

docs.title: ADR-0007: Export Regular and Clear as built-in Glass styles
ADR-0007: Export Regular and Clear as built-in Glass styles
docs.text: Haze will expose GlassStyle.regular and GlassStyle.clear as shared built-in styles rather than adding a public modifier variant parameter or extending the public GlassOptics API with semantic cases. The parallel sample-only preset catalogue will be removed rather than retained or exported. Regular remains the default size-responsive material. Clear initially used size-responsive blur and depth with an authored refraction response, and remains recognisably distinct when a renderer simplifies advanced optics. Both styles own the complete optical, edge, lighting, chromatic, tone, and content-normal response while preserving independently composed shape, background colour, tint, alpha, light position, and interaction appearance. These are Haze styles informed by iOS's semantic distinction and measured direction, not promises of pixel parity or Apple-internal constants. Identity remains outside this decision because disabling attachment and rendering is modifier/runtime behaviour rather than a Glass appearance.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Callers select a built-in response through the existing replayable Style seam and customize it with then, without learning another public type or precedence rule. Switching between Regular and Clear resets every built-in-style-owned channel but does not erase theme or caller presentation. Samples use Regular and Clear directly; sample-only Adaptive, Clear, Frosted, Deep, and Prism presets are removed. A sample that teaches custom authoring declares that customization locally instead of adding another reusable preset catalogue.

ADR-0008 revises the representation of their optics: Regular and Clear remain built-in Glass styles, but their optical behavior is expressible through the same public configuration available to callers.

docs.title: Diffusion calibration, 2026-09-16
docs.text:
Clear now uses constant shallow diffusion: OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(1f) for depth and OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(1.25.dp) for blur radius. This supersedes the size-responsive Clear response above. Native UIKit captures on iOS 27.0 (24A434), built with Xcode 27.0 (27A266a) and SDK 27.0, use the same 64/176/220pt geometry and 8pt grid as Haze's size fixture. The simulator's Liquid Glass preference is Default (Tint Amount 50%); Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast are disabled. Clear retains approximately 23/27/28% of the unfiltered grid's adjacent-pixel linear-luminance contrast. Light and dark Clear captures agree. This replaces the initial iOS 26 calibration, whose more diffuse Clear reference led to a provisional 2dp radius.

Regular retains approximately 24% on the compact capsule and effectively none on the larger native surfaces. An independent launch reproduces that response. Haze keeps its compact diffusion and increases the 176/220dp depth anchors to 0.98/1, reducing the sharp-source contribution on cards and removing it on panels. Its 64dp depth remains 0.85 and its blur radii remain 4/10/15dp.

These are empirical diffusion targets, not Apple-specified radii or a pixel-parity contract. The metric includes tone and refraction as well as blur, and native Regular's adaptive appearance and edge treatment differ. The calibration prioritizes stronger diffusion on larger Regular surfaces. Both styles continue to use the existing public optics configuration; no renderer-specific identity branch or additional API is needed.

docs.title: Clear refraction calibration, 2026-09-16
docs.text:
A separate four-phase native capture isolates apparent sampling displacement from the grid's repeating lines. Clear now selects RefractionProfile.Edge(28.dp), with strength 0.85 and authored displacement 56dp. The fitted inward decay and optical corner radius (1.5 times the visible radius, capped at half the shortest side) reproduce the accepted corner loops. Displacement is capped at half the shortest side. The production normal is analytic rather than four additional distance samples per pixel. Lighting retains Circle, with height fraction 0.35; white point is 0.17.

RefractionProfile.Surface remains the default for caller-authored optics. This explicit profile preserves existing surface semantics; Edge width controls refraction independently of the surface height used for lighting. Both base and interaction detail use the same sampling map. Zero width disables Edge sampling and its detail pass.

These settings are an empirical visual match for the accepted fixture, not Apple's implementation or a promise of parity across content.

docs.title: Regular refraction and wide diffusion calibration, 2026-09-16
docs.text:
Further grid and photographic comparisons supersede the provisional Regular settings above. Regular now uses Edge(20.dp) with authored 48dp displacement at 0.7 strength, lighting height fraction 0.15, and no secondary detail or fold. Depth is 0.65/1/1 and blur is 20/24/25dp at 64/176/220dp. Compact controls retain refracted grid loops; cards and panels remove both fine grid lines and medium-scale photographic detail. The light-appearance tone uses white point 0.55 and chroma multiplier 1.5, with ambient response 0.15 and edge softness 1dp. Clear's accepted settings remain unchanged.

This exposed a source-space blur cap of 38.5 physical pixels: larger authored radii previously produced the same result at dense resolutions. Non-progressive blur now supports up to 256px. Both backends use native Gaussian filtering for uniform blur above four input pixels so input bounds include all required samples, including lower-density Performance rendering. The custom runtime-filter paths exposed sharp backdrop strips near output boundaries. Android retains one fused output graph; the retained Skiko path caches the native filter and its blurred layer. Small-radius and progressive blur keep their semantic kernels, and progressive blur retains its previous radius bound. Layer budgets and lifecycle follow the selected backend path. This wide-blur correctness exception to ADR-0003 has host pixel coverage; its physical-device performance has not been measured.

Native light and dark appearances differ substantially. The original fixed Haze response targeted the light reference; subsequent system appearance support selects separate light and dark responses at node resolution. The comparisons establish visual direction, not physical GPU performance or native content adaptation.

docs.title: System appearance response, 2026-09-23
docs.text:
Regular and Clear remain shared, immutable Style values. A built-in records an appearance-dependent write in its ordered replay sequence, and the attached Glass node reads the Compose host's system appearance. This also applies to the implicit Regular response when style is omitted. A live host appearance change replays the sequence and invalidates affected rendering without reconstructing caller Styles. Later writes retain precedence, and a later built-in resets its owned channels while preserving shape, background, tint, alpha, light position, and interactions.

The light response retains the 2026-09-16 calibration. The dark response lowers white point and ambient lift and changes edge and highlight balance while retaining Regular's size-dependent diffusion and Clear's shallow, more transparent optics. These are Haze approximations, not iOS pixel matches or Apple coefficients. Material 3 remains a separate optional builder for app-theme surface color and tint. The host may override device appearance; an unknown Skiko theme uses the light response. The pinned Skiko theme local is internal and deprecated, so Compose upgrades must recheck that adapter.

The new dark references use a 64/176/220dp capsule/card/panel fixture at 1dp per pixel, with a structured dark grid for Regular and a bright photograph for Clear. Desktop captures use a 420×800px Skiko host; Android host captures use the Pixel 5 Robolectric profile at SDK 28, 32, and 35. Each style also passes a light→dark→light capture on the same attached node: more than 1% of pixels change, and the restored image differs from the initial image by less than one 8-bit color step on average. The Android SDK 28 path exercises fallback rendering. These checks establish Haze output and reversibility under controlled host appearance; they do not establish physical-device behavior, a manual OS switch, or a side-by-side native dark match.

docs.title: Colour handling, 2026-09-17
docs.text:
chromaMultiplier above 1f is a requested chroma boost, bounded for source colours already in the sRGB gamut. A boost that would leave that gamut is reduced to the in-gamut limit, and an already out-of-gamut source is left unchanged. The purpose is source-colour preservation: clamping an amplified saturated colour would create a broad colour plateau that loses the original hue and detail.

Authored tint and edgeShadow retain Compose ColorSpace semantics through colour-managed shader uniforms on supported renderers. This decision does not settle the whole colour model: encoded luma() used to construct content normals, display-space contrast, and ambient multiplication remain explicitly deferred questions rather than claims of scene-linear behaviour.

docs.title: Represent responsive Glass optics as public configuration
Represent responsive Glass optics as public configuration
docs.text: GlassOptics will be one immutable configuration value rather than a sealed choice between Adaptive and Fixed. Its blur radius and depth each own an independent OpticalSizeValue<T>: either a Fixed value or a Responsive value containing two or more OpticalSizePoint<T> values. Each point pairs a strictly increasing shortest dimension with one parameter value; values interpolate with smoothstep and clamp outside the authored range. This makes responsive optics a public customization capability, lets parameters use different size points, and lets Regular and Clear use the same model as caller-authored styles without subtype or identity-based behavior.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Regular uses authored refraction constants of 48.dp displacement and 0.6f height rather than its previous private aspect-ratio and roundness adjustments. refractionDetailIntensity becomes a validated public optical value so Regular can select 0f and Clear can select 0.76f without hidden runtime distinctions. Responsive-value points are snapshotted and rejected unless they contain at least two valid points in strictly increasing dimension order. This revises ADR-0007's optics boundary without changing its decision to expose Regular and Clear as built-in Glass styles.

OpticalSizeValue.Fixed<T> and OpticalSizeValue.Responsive<T> are single-field domain values and therefore use @JvmInline value class; the responsive variant snapshots its public constructor input before the init block validates it. OpticalSizePoint<T> and GlassOptics remain data classes because they contain multiple independent values. The generic containers deliberately do not carry @Immutable, because callers may instantiate them with a mutable T; GlassOptics retains that annotation because its public properties constrain T to Float and Dp. Using the variants through OpticalSizeValue<T> may box them, so this choice states the domain model rather than promising an allocation optimization.

docs.title: Use opt-in Android window backdrops
docs.text:
Haze will expose HazeInput.Backdrop(fallback: HazeInput.Sources) as an experimental input. On a supported hardware-accelerated Android window, built-in effects may filter pixels already drawn behind the effect through a dedicated RenderNode. The fallback is mandatory and remains the authoritative result on older Android releases, other platforms, unsupported renderers, and after native setup or drawing fails.

Backdrop input is not another source-selection policy. It samples the combined earlier pixels in the current window surface; it cannot select individual Haze sources, include later drawing, or cross a dialog, popup, or window boundary. Callers that require those semantics continue to use HazeInput.Sources directly.

Core owns attachment-scoped backend selection, geometry, clipping, transforms, draw ordering, and fallback capture demand. A missing capability, unavailable canvas, unusable root effect, or native failure selects source fallback until the modifier node detaches. A healthy native node neither allocates nor records its fallback source layers. This keeps fallback reliable without charging the native path for dormant capture work.

The Android platform renderer is gated on the full 37.2 SDK version and hardware acceleration, not major API 37 alone. Its backend and built-in renderer capability remain internal; callers cannot select a backend or supply a custom backdrop root effect through the supported public API.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Existing HazeInput.Sources and HazeInput.Content behavior is unchanged. Blur and Glass retain ownership of their complete platform effect graphs and may opt into the internal capability only when their styling can be represented without weakening their public contract. A native-to-source transition may take one frame, but known failures are not retried every frame.

ADR-0003 remains authoritative for source-backed Android Glass. Backdrop is an explicit input exception: it may reuse the fused effect graph, but it must not replace or simplify the retained source-backed renderer.

docs.title: Adopt Backdrop as the adaptive Haze input
Adopt Backdrop as the adaptive Haze input
docs.text:
HazeInput.Sources remains the exact source-capture input. HazeInput.Backdrop is the normal input for a built-in Blur or Glass surface whose intent is to consume the pixels already drawn behind it in the current window:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
)

The native path samples the combined earlier pixels in the same window surface. It cannot select individual Haze sources, include later drawing, or cross a dialog, popup, or other window boundary. When the native path is unavailable, Haze uses Backdrop's fallback source input when one is supplied. HazeInput.Backdrop() has no portable source fallback: content remains unchanged and Haze does not demand source capture. A supplied fallback's selection and retention policies apply only to that source-capture path; they do not filter native window pixels.

docs.title: Eligibility and fallback
docs.text:
HazeFeatureFlags.isPlatformBackdropEnabled is an experimental process-wide switch. It is false by default. Set it before attaching the Haze effect nodes that should observe the switch:

HazeFeatureFlags.isPlatformBackdropEnabled = true

The switch makes the platform renderer eligible; it does not force native rendering. Built-in effect support, the Android full 37.2 SDK gate, the current window and canvas, native setup, and native drawing must all succeed. Unsupported platforms, incompatible effects, software canvases, and setup or draw failures use a supplied source fallback. Without a fallback, content remains unchanged and Haze does not demand source capture. A known unavailable or failed native path remains sticky until that modifier node detaches. Existing attached nodes keep the value observed at attachment; a later attachment reads the current value.

The current implementation is experimental and has not established physical Android 37.2 acceptance or a performance result. Those remain release gates. The rollout is deliberately staged: after acceptance a later release may enable the default, retain false temporarily as a regression escape hatch, and then remove the flag.

docs.title: Diagnostics and consequences
docs.text:
Enable HazeLogger.enabled while diagnosing selection and fallback messages. Native draw work is also marked by the HazeBackdrop.draw trace section. These are diagnostics, not a public backend selection or status API.

On a healthy native attachment, Haze does not record dormant source layers. A native-to-source transition may take one frame when a fallback is supplied; that fallback remains responsible for portable rendering and retained-output behavior. ADR-0009 records the earlier wrapper-based decision and remains unchanged as historical context; this ADR supersedes its public input shape.

docs.title: Evaluate Glass styles under state observation
Evaluate Glass styles under state observation
docs.text:
A GlassStyle block currently runs exactly once, when the style is built. Its values are validated and recorded at that point, and the recorded writes are replayed into each node later. To animate a Glass shape, for example a button morphing into a menu, a caller has to build a new style on every frame, which recomposes the hazeGlass call site each time (#1408).

Glass styles will instead follow the evaluation model of Compose Foundation Styles (androidx.compose.foundation.style). The node evaluates the style block itself and observes the snapshot state the block reads. When that state changes, the node resolves the style again and invalidates only the affected work, without recomposition. Built-in styles, LocalGlassStyle, then and the order in which later writes win stay the same.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Implement Compose's CustomStyle<GlassStyleScope> directly. Rejected. Haze's public styling API would then inherit @ExperimentalFoundationStyleApi and the stability of foundation's types. Haze copies the semantics using its own GlassStyle and GlassStyleScope types instead.
  • Add per-frame lambdas for a few named properties, or a separate modifier-level block. Rejected. Either would give Glass two ways to set the same appearance value, each with its own precedence rules, and would diverge from the Compose model that callers already know.
  • Move Glass interaction responses to pressed {}, hovered {} and animate {} blocks. Deferred. The interaction API is unchanged by this decision.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The block's contract changes. The documentation that says the block "executes exactly once" no longer holds. A block may run on any frame, so it must not have side effects.
  • Validation moves to evaluation time, with coercion for animated values. Alpha and tint alpha are clamped to 0..1 and negative corner radii to zero, so animation overshoot can't throw during draw. Non-finite corner radii keep using the safe-default fallback. Other invalid values still throw IllegalArgumentException, now when the block runs.
  • No property has a guaranteed-cheap invalidation path. Every property can be driven by state, and a change invalidates the stages its dirty fields map to, which for shape, alpha and tint still includes layer bounds and delegate selection. The original decision promised that those three would skip that work. A physical-device measurement (#1408) found the skipped work would cost about 0.004 ms per effect per frame on a shape-and-size morph, where the size change pays it anyway. The narrowing (#1420) was dropped. Revisit it only if a measurement, such as a radius-only animation at constant size, shows a meaningful cost.
  • Some changes always pay the broader cost. These can change the retained-layer plan:
  • Corner radii crossing zero change the clip decision.
  • Alpha entering or leaving the fractional range 0 < alpha < 1 adds or removes the full-size group-composite layer. That layer counts against the render budget, so the change can select a different renderer.
  • Alpha reaching zero skips drawing altogether.
  • Placement re-evaluates the style only when the effect's size changes. The style resolves against the effect size, so a resize runs the block again. A change of position or transform alone, whether the effect or its source moves, updates only the effect's geometry and does not run the block (#1456).

docs.title: Do not guarantee frozen pixels for retained Glass output
Do not guarantee frozen pixels for retained Glass output
docs.text:
HazeSourceRetention.KeepLastFrame keeps drawing retained output when selected sources become unavailable. On Android, retained Glass output is a replayed layer, not an immutable image. It can redraw from live source content after source selection is lost or a source detaches while the material is hidden, and it can show descendant changes made after capture (#1405).

Haze will document this limit instead of guaranteeing frozen last-displayed pixels. KeepLastFrame promises smooth source transitions, not a pixel-exact snapshot. ClearWhenUnavailable remains the policy for surfaces where stale or live source pixels must not appear.

The shared HazeSourceRetention contract is narrowed for every effect and platform, because Haze makes no frozen-pixel guarantee anywhere. The observed leak is limited to Android Glass; Blur and JVM/Skiko retention were not investigated for it.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Always capture immutable input images. Rejected for now. The prototype in #1383 fixed the source-loss cases, but raised nine-effect CPU frame P90 on a Pixel 8a from about 6.0–6.2 ms to 8.3–8.6 ms, with CPU placement uncontrolled. It also clipped Display-P3 sources to sRGB.
  • A cheaper always-on immutable capture. Deferred. No candidate exists yet that meets the performance bar below. HardwareBufferRenderer with RGBA_FP16 preserved Display-P3 on API 37, and is a starting point for future work.
  • Capture only when a source is about to disappear. Rejected. The pixels can already be gone, for example when a source detaches while the material is hidden.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No runtime cost. The KeepLastFrame KDoc and the Glass, core-concepts and Blur usage docs state the limit.
  • Two stacked or nested material failures from #1405 have an unknown root cause. This decision does not address them, and they remain uninvestigated.
  • A future capture path must clear the #1373 bar of no ongoing overhead beyond measurement noise, preserve the Glass colour-handling contract, and supersede this decision.

docs.title: Merge nearby Glass surfaces through a container
Merge nearby Glass surfaces through a container
docs.text:
On iOS, Liquid Glass elements inside a GlassEffectContainer blend into one shape when they come within the container's spacing. Elements that are inserted or removed morph out of, or back into, their neighbours. Haze couldn't do either, because each hazeGlass node draws its own layer from the signed distance field of a single rounded rectangle (#1409). A prototype (#1438) showed that the existing optics hold on a smooth minimum of member shapes. It needed three fixes:

  • fade refraction across thin bridges;
  • fade smoothing as members overlap, so a full overlap ends at their union;
  • stop sizing optics from the inflated layer.

Haze will add Modifier.hazeGlassContainer(spacing, transitionSpec, reducedMotionPolicy). spacing is required and has no default. Ordinary hazeGlass modifiers below it become Glass members of their nearest container, and the container draws every member's glass behind its own children. A member's own style still sets its shape, input and appearance.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
• Members whose gap is less than half the spacing join into a Glass cluster. The container draws each cluster as one surface, shaped by a polynomial smooth minimum with k = spacing. Members outside every cluster draw as separate surfaces.
  • A cluster merges at most four members, because shapes reach the shader as fixed-size uniform arrays. Beyond four, the extra members draw on their own without a bridge, in a deterministic order. Where an extra member overlaps the cluster, blur and tint apply twice in the overlap, which is the visible cost of the cap.
  • A cluster draws at one z-position, so only members registered consecutively share a surface. A member registered between two compatible neighbours splits them, even when it is far away, so merging never reorders members.
  • Members can merge only when their input, performance mode and material values are equal: optics, surface profile, specular and edge response, chromatic aberration, tone, light position and alpha. Values that belong to each member are excluded from that comparison: shape, tint, backgroundColor and interaction responses. Each member keeps its own shape, colours and interaction response, and the colours blend across the bridge. As a result, Regular and Clear surfaces never merge.
  • The container resolves one optical size: the largest shortest side among all its members. Every member evaluates its own optics at that size, whether or not it is in a cluster. When the size changes because a member was added, removed or resized, it changes immediately and is not animated. A member that is leaving does not count.
  • Each member's interaction transform and interaction lighting apply to that member's part of the field. Pressing one member can shrink it within the merged shape (interaction scales are at most 1), and only that member brightens.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
Members have no identifiers, because a Compose modifier node already keeps one identity for as long as it is attached. Each member chooses a transition:

  • MatchedGeometry is the default. A member that attaches within the spacing of another member grows out of it. A member that detaches retracts into it, while the container keeps drawing its shape until the animation ends.
  • Materialize fades the glass in or out where it is. MatchedGeometry also falls back to it beyond the spacing.
  • None applies no transition.

A morph starts or ends on the neighbour's drawn outline: its rect after its interaction transform, with its corners scaled as they are drawn. A pressed neighbour therefore stays continuous with the member growing out of it or retracting into it. Spacing and neighbour checks still ignore interaction transforms. A member chooses a growing neighbour by its current morph, and keeps that link while either the morph or the neighbour's layout is within the spacing.

A member with HazeInput.Content input leaves immediately, without a ghost, because the content its glass samples leaves with it (#1485).

Haze doesn't animate member content, so callers fade content themselves.

Under reduced motion, the transition keeps its morph but uses a critically damped animation instead of the spring, so it doesn't overshoot. reducedMotionPolicy uses the existing GlassReducedMotionPolicy values. When GlassReducedMotionPolicy.System sees a zero platform motion scale (animations off), member transitions snap instead (#1560).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Members registering through an explicit state object. Rejected. It matches the HazeState pattern, but adds a public type and mismatch cases. Finding the nearest ancestor needs neither.
  • A container that declares the input and style. Rejected. Shape is a style property and members need their own shapes. Ignoring some style values inside a container would also give Glass two places to declare a material.
  • Merging only identical styles. Rejected. iOS merges elements with different tints. Comparing style instances would also break merging for an inline GlassStyle {} block, which creates a new instance whenever its call site recomposes.
  • Sizing optics from the smallest member, or per cluster. Rejected. iOS sizes optics per container, so a small control next to a large panel takes on the panel's diffusion even when the two don't merge.
  • One layer covering every member. Rejected. A sparse container would pay for a container-sized layer while nothing merges.
  • Snapping transitions under reduced motion. Rejected for GlassReducedMotionPolicy.Reduced. iOS keeps the morph and removes its elasticity. Turning animations off is different: GlassReducedMotionPolicy.System snaps at a zero platform motion scale (#1560).
  • glassEffectID-style identifiers and glassEffectUnion-style forced unions. Deferred. Identifiers add nothing over node identity for neighbour morphs. A forced union needs grouping rules that the first version doesn't need.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Where Glass samples from changes inside a container. It sits behind all of the container's children, so with backdrop input it samples only content drawn before the container. Joining or leaving a cluster never moves a member in z-order, and hazeGlass outside a container is unchanged.
  • Optics depend on the container's members. A small member next to a large one shows the large member's diffusion even when the two don't merge. Adding or removing the large member changes the small one's optics immediately.
  • A cluster is one Glass surface for the renderer. This narrows ADR-0003's ownership rule from one node to one drawn surface. On Android API 33 and newer, each cluster owns one source capture and one fused output, built as ADR-0003 describes. Skiko and environments without RuntimeShader keep their existing adapters. An isolated member is a cluster of one. The container decides which members share a surface, but renderer selection still doesn't depend on member or sibling count.
  • The renderer gains shader inputs and new uniform plumbing. The new shader inputs are the merged field, per-member colours, interaction transforms and lights, which needs an array setter for runtime-shader uniforms. In reduced-quality modes, merged silhouettes follow single surfaces and render at the reduced input scale. Full-resolution silhouettes are out of scope (#1339).
  • The dome term is disabled for clusters. It is defined only for a single rounded rectangle.
  • The fallback renderer draws no bridge. It renders each cluster as one surface clipped to the hard union of the member shapes, so overlapping members of a cluster never double their blur or tint. Members beyond the cap still draw separately.
  • A system animation-scale change applies from the next transition. A transition that is already running continues as it started.
  • A retract into a neighbour whose style alpha the caller animates ends immediately. Alpha is part of the merge key, so the neighbour is no longer compatible once its alpha changes.
  • Merging costs extra GPU work. On a Pixel 8a, two merged pills finished frames about 1.2–1.5 ms later at P50 and P90 than the same pills drawn independently, with a layer about three times the area. CPU frame time was within noise. These were single sessions, and CPU frame time does not measure GPU shader cost.
  • Lazy layouts pass their scroll state. Compose gives a modifier no signal that tells a scroll-driven attach from a state-driven one. Callers pass the lazy layout's ScrollableState to hazeGlassContainer, and members attach and detach without a transition while it scrolls. The default stays MatchedGeometry (#1485). Inferring scrolls from member positions was measured and rejected: a uniform state-driven shift looks like a scroll, and a scroll past the viewport leaves no evidence (#1524).

docs.title: Blur Effect
docs.text: Blur creates a frosted-glass effect over content in your UI. It can blur the content behind a surface, or a composable's own content.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    // Core library infrastructure
    implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze:<version>")

    // Blur effect
    implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur:<version>")

    // Optional: Pre-built blur styles
    implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur-materials:<version>")
}

docs.title: Platform Support
docs.text:
Blur is available on every platform Haze supports:

Platform Notes Android Android 6.0 (API 23)+. Blurs by default on Android 12+; a translucent scrim is drawn on Android 11 and below unless you opt in. Desktop (JVM) Full support. iOS & macOS Full support. Web (Wasm, JS) Full support.

See Platforms for details.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Mark the content to blur with hazeSource, then apply Modifier.hazeBlur to the surface drawn over it:

val hazeState = rememberHazeState()
val style = HazeMaterials.thin()

Box {
    LazyColumn(
        modifier = Modifier
            .fillMaxSize()
            .hazeSource(state = hazeState)
    ) {
        // scrollable content
    }

    TopAppBar(
        modifier = Modifier.hazeBlur(
            input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
            style = style,
        ),
    )
}

See the Blur usage guide for more.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
HazeBlurStyle controls how Blur looks:

  • Blur radius: the strength of the blur.
  • Tint: a color overlay that improves contrast.
  • Noise: visual texture.

For ready-made styles, see the material presets. To follow the current Material 3 theme, see the Material 3 integration.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Blur can be expensive. See Performance for how to measure and tune it.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Blur usage: inputs, styles, progressive Blur, and masks
  • Material presets: ready-made Blur Styles
  • Material 3 integration: a Blur Style from your Material 3 theme
  • Performance: measuring and tuning

docs.title: What's the difference between this and Modifier.blur?
docs.text:
Modifier.blur blurs a composable's own content. Haze's main use is blurring the content behind a surface, which is what glass-like effects need. Haze can also blur a composable's own content with HazeInput.Content.

Haze also adds tints, noise, progressive Blur, masks, and more. See the Usage page.

docs.title: Why does my Blur get clipped inside a graphics layer?
docs.text:
An enclosing graphicsLayer that uses alpha below one, an offscreen compositing strategy, a color filter, or similar options clips its content to its bounds. Blur that spreads past those bounds is cut off.

Use Compose 1.12's LayerOutsets on that enclosing layer, on the edges that need the extra space. For Blur that can spread equally on every edge, match each outset to the Blur radius:

val blurRadius = 32.dp

Box(
  Modifier.graphicsLayer(
    alpha = 0.5f,
    outsets = LayerOutsets(blurRadius, blurRadius, blurRadius, blurRadius),
  ),
) {
  Box(
    Modifier.hazeBlur(
      input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
      style = HazeBlurStyle { blurRadius(blurRadius) },
    ),
  )
}

Outsets only enlarge the area the layer can draw into; they don't change what Haze blurs. An explicit clip still applies.

docs.title: Does Blur look the same on every platform?
docs.text: Yes, with the same API on every platform. The exceptions are on older Android versions: Android 12 and 12L approximate some progressive Blur, and Android 11 and below draw a scrim unless you enable Blur. See Platforms.

docs.title: What versions of Android does Haze work on?
docs.text: See the Platforms page.

docs.title: When should I use Backdrop instead of Sources?
docs.text: Use HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState) for most Blur: it blurs whatever was drawn earlier in the same window. Use HazeInput.Sources(hazeState) when you need to choose exactly which sources are blurred, blur content from another window, or control what is shown while sources are unavailable. See Blur usage for details, including the experimental native Android backdrop.

docs.title: Material 3 integration
docs.text:
The haze-blur-material3 artifact creates a Blur Style from your current Material 3 theme. For ready-made presets, see Blur material presets.

dependencies {
  implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur-material3:<version>")
}

HazeBlurStyle.Material3() uses MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surface as the background color. Pass containerColor to use a different color. An optional block runs afterwards, so it can override any property, including the background:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = HazeBlurStyle.Material3 {
    blurRadius(12.dp)
  },
)

To apply it to every Blur in a subtree, provide it through LocalHazeBlurStyle:

CompositionLocalProvider(LocalHazeBlurStyle provides HazeBlurStyle.Material3()) {
  // Blur modifiers in this subtree inherit the Material 3 surface background.
}

docs.title: Blur material presets
docs.text:
The haze-blur-materials artifact provides ready-made Blur Styles in Haze, Cupertino, and Fluent designs:

dependencies {
  implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur-materials:<version>")
}

For a Style that follows your Material 3 theme, see the Material 3 integration.

docs.title: Material
docs.text:
HazeMaterials provides ultraThin(), thin(), regular(), thick(), and ultraThick():

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = HazeMaterials.thin(),
)

docs.title: Cupertino
docs.text:
CupertinoMaterials follows Apple platform materials:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = CupertinoMaterials.regular(),
)

docs.title: Fluent
docs.text:
FluentMaterials provides acrylic and Mica presets:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = FluentMaterials.acrylicDefault(),
)

docs.title: Customizing a preset
docs.text:
Presets are ordinary Styles. Use then to override individual properties:

val compact = HazeMaterials.thin().then {
  blurRadius(12.dp)
  noiseFactor(0f)
}

The result can be shared between modifiers.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text:
Haze works on every platform Compose Multiplatform supports: Android, iOS, macOS, Desktop (JVM), and Web (Wasm and JS).

Compose Multiplatform platforms

Compose Multiplatform supports fewer platforms than Kotlin Multiplatform. Haze can only support a platform once Compose Multiplatform does.

docs.title: Android
docs.text: Haze supports Android 6.0 (API 23) and newer.

docs.title: Android 13+
docs.text:
SDK Levels: 33+

All features are fully supported.

docs.title: Android 12 & 12L
docs.text:
SDK Levels: 31 & 32

Blur is enabled by default, with these differences:

docs.title: HazeProgressive
docs.text:
With a full-resolution performance mode, such as HazePerformanceMode.Quality, linear HazeProgressive effects are drawn several times. This costs more, so measure it for your workload.

Lower-resolution modes, such as HazePerformanceMode.Balanced, and all non-linear progressive types use a gradient mask instead. This blends between blurred and unblurred content rather than varying the blur strength.

docs.title: Extra redraws
docs.text:
On Android 12 (API 31) and below, Haze redraws Blur more often than strictly necessary so that it stays in sync with the content behind it.

On API 31 only, Blur that reads HazeInput.Sources, including a HazeInput.Backdrop using its source fallback, also recaptures its input after any snapshot state change in the app, whichever window holds the source. With a hardware-accelerated canvas, Blur also rebuilds all of its effects, including every progressive band. With a software canvas, it blurs again with RenderScript instead. A running animation therefore does this once per frame, even if the animation is unrelated to the content behind the Blur. Blur that uses HazeInput.Content is not affected. This cost has not been measured. If you target API 31, profile your screens and disable Blur where it is too slow.

Sources in another window also recapture their input on every snapshot change on other API levels, and on platforms where Haze detects separate windows. See Dialogs.

docs.title: Android 11 and below
docs.text:
SDK Levels: 30 and below

Blur is disabled by default. Haze draws a translucent scrim instead:

The scrim has no blurred content to filter. It draws a HazeColorEffect.colorFilter(...) as a white scrim passed through the filter, using the effect's blend mode, so a color filter that is the first color effect or the fallbackColorEffect may not look as intended. Set a tint as the fallbackColorEffect for a predictable scrim.

docs.title: RenderScript blurring
docs.text:
You can enable Blur on these versions, which uses RenderScript.

Experimental

Blur on Android 11 and below is experimental. It may become the default in a future release, or be removed if it proves unstable. Please raise issues if you find problems.

This path is slower than on Android 12 and newer. To avoid dropping frames, Haze blurs on a background thread and skips frames while it is busy, so the Blur usually trails content changes by a frame or more. It can look laggy when the content behind it changes quickly. Progressive Blur uses a gradient mask, as described above.

RenderScript draws noise over the blur at the noise factor's opacity. On API 31 and newer with hardware acceleration, and on other platforms, noise uses the soft-light blend mode. The grain therefore looks different on the RenderScript path. API 31 and newer also use that path when the canvas is not hardware accelerated.

A HazeColorEffect.colorFilter(...) filters the blurred output, as it does on Android 12 and newer and on Skiko. It also filters the noise and any color effects before it in the list.

Thanks

Big thanks to Serhii Yaremych for his help on this, as we have managed to get an optimized 'content write' working. 🚀

docs.title: Desktop
docs.text: Desktop (JVM) is fully supported. See Skiko platforms.

docs.title: iOS
docs.text: iOS is fully supported. See Skiko platforms.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: macOS is supported on Apple silicon (macosArm64). See Skiko platforms.

docs.title: Web
docs.text: Web is fully supported on Kotlin/Wasm and Kotlin/JS. See Skiko platforms.

docs.title: Skiko
docs.text:
Desktop, iOS, macOS, and Web all render through Skiko, which bundles the Skia Graphics Library into your app. Blur behaves the same on all of them: every feature is supported and Blur is enabled by default.

Haze is built, tested, and released against the latest stable version of Compose Multiplatform.

docs.title: Using pre-release versions of Compose Multiplatform
docs.text: We occasionally verify against pre-release versions of Compose Multiplatform, but don't guarantee compatibility. Test thoroughly if you use one.

docs.title: Blur usage
docs.text: Modifier.hazeBlur takes an input, which decides what gets blurred, and a Style, which decides how it looks.

docs.title: Choosing the input
docs.text:
Requirement Input What it blurs Blur whatever is behind a surface HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState) Content drawn earlier in the same window, using your hazeSource content where native backdrop rendering isn't used. Control exactly which sources are blurred HazeInput.Sources(hazeState) Content marked with selected hazeSource modifiers. Blur the modifier's own content HazeInput.Content The composable's own content.

Use Backdrop for most cases.

docs.title: Source-backed Blur
docs.text:
val hazeState = rememberHazeState()
val style = HazeMaterials.thin()

Box {
  LazyColumn(
    modifier = Modifier
      .fillMaxSize()
      .hazeSource(hazeState),
  ) {
    // Content
  }

  TopAppBar(
    modifier = Modifier.hazeBlur(
      input = HazeInput.Sources(hazeState),
      style = style,
    ),
  )
}

HazeInput.Sources also controls which sources are used and what is shown while they are unavailable. The default, KeepLastFrame, avoids an empty flash during source transitions, but the retained output is not guaranteed to be an exact copy of the last frame (see Core concepts). Use ClearWhenUnavailable for privacy-sensitive content:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Sources(
    state = hazeState,
    retention = HazeSourceRetention.ClearWhenUnavailable,
  ),
)

docs.title: Own-content Blur
docs.text:
Use HazeInput.Content when the modifier's own content is the input:

Image(
  modifier = Modifier.hazeBlur(
    input = HazeInput.Content,
    style = HazeMaterials.thin(),
  ),
)

docs.title: Android window-backdrop Blur
docs.text:
On Android 37.2 or later, HazeInput.Backdrop can blur the window backdrop natively. This is experimental and off by default. Enable it before the Blur modifiers you want to affect are attached:

HazeFeatureFlags.isPlatformBackdropEnabled = true

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = HazeMaterials.thin(),
)

Enabling the flag makes native rendering possible, not guaranteed. On other platforms, older Android releases, a software canvas, or if native rendering fails, Haze uses your hazeSource content instead; switching can take one frame. Changing the flag only affects modifiers attached afterwards.

Native rendering blurs content drawn earlier in the same window. It can't see content drawn later, or content in another dialog, popup, or window, and HazePerformanceMode doesn't reduce its resolution. Use HazeInput.Sources when you need exact source selection, content from another window, or a retention policy.

Set HazeLogger.enabled = true to log which path is chosen. A later release may enable native rendering by default.

docs.title: Enabling Blur
docs.text:
Blur is enabled by default on Android 12 and newer and on all other platforms. On Android 11 and below, Haze draws a translucent scrim instead unless you enable Blur (see Platforms). To override the default, set blurEnabled in a Style:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = HazeBlurStyle {
    blurEnabled(true)
  },
)

When Blur is disabled, Haze draws fallbackColorEffect instead.

docs.title: Replayable Styles
docs.text:
A HazeBlurStyle is a list of property writes:

val style = HazeBlurStyle {
  blurEnabled(true)
  blurRadius(20.dp)
  noiseFactor(0.15f)
  backgroundColor(Color.Black)
  colorEffects(
    listOf(
      HazeColorEffect.tint(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.12f)),
    ),
  )
  fallbackColorEffect(HazeColorEffect.tint(Color.Black.copy(alpha = 0.7f)))
  alpha(1f)
  mask(null)
  progressive(null)
  blurredEdgeTreatment(BlurredEdgeTreatment.Rectangle)
}

Haze applies Styles in this order:

  1. HazeBlurDefaults.style
  2. LocalHazeBlurStyle
  3. The explicit hazeBlur Style

The last write to a property wins, both across tiers and within a Style chain:

val compact = HazeMaterials.thin().then {
  blurRadius(12.dp)
  noiseFactor(0f)
}

Properties a Style doesn't write keep their inherited value. Styles are immutable and safe to share; create a new Style to change the appearance.

colorEffects copies the list you pass, so later changes to your list have no effect. An empty list clears inherited color effects:

val noColorEffects = HazeBlurStyle {
  colorEffects(emptyList())
}

docs.title: Progressive Blur and masks
docs.text:
Progressive Blur varies intensity across the surface:

val progressiveStyle = HazeBlurStyle {
  progressive(
    HazeProgressive.verticalGradient(
      startIntensity = 1f,
      endIntensity = 0f,
    ),
  )
}

A mask fades the effect's opacity instead, and is usually cheaper:

val maskedStyle = HazeBlurStyle {
  mask(
    Brush.verticalGradient(
      colors = listOf(Color.Black, Color.Transparent),
    ),
  )
}

The two can be combined. Progressive Blur varies the intensity first, then the mask fades the complete result, so fully transparent mask regions show no effect:

val maskedProgressiveStyle = HazeBlurStyle {
  progressive(HazeProgressive.horizontalGradient())
  mask(
    Brush.verticalGradient(
      colors = listOf(Color.Black, Color.Transparent),
    ),
  )
}

On Android 12L and below, progressive Blur is approximated (see Platforms).

docs.title: Performance mode and layer expansion
docs.text:
Performance mode and layer expansion are hazeBlur parameters, not Style properties:

Modifier.hazeBlur(
  input = HazeInput.Sources(hazeState),
  style = style,
  performanceMode = HazePerformanceMode.Default,
  expandLayerBounds = true,
)

See the performance guide for choosing a mode, and Blur guidance for when to change expandLayerBounds. Measured results are in the benchmark results.

docs.title: Glass
docs.text: A refraction-driven Glass effect that combines refraction, depth blur, tint, Fresnel/ambient lift, and specular highlights with optional rounded shapes and dispersion.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
Glass is published to Maven Central starting with Haze 2.0.0-alpha04. Use the same version for the core and Glass artifacts:

dependencies {
    implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze:<version>")
    implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-glass:<version>")
}

For unreleased changes, follow the snapshot build instructions and use the same snapshot version for both artifacts.

docs.title: Material 3
docs.text:
Add the optional Material 3 integration when a Glass surface should use the current theme surface color:

dependencies {
  implementation("dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-glass-material3:<version>")
}

material3() uses MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surface as its background color. Pass containerColor to use a different color. It leaves the tint unset unless you pass one. It is composable, so the Style follows theme changes when the call site recomposes.

Material 3 supplies only colors. Regular and Clear still pick their light or dark response from the system appearance, not from MaterialTheme, and you don't need Material 3 for that.

Apply Material 3 to a built-in or custom Style with material3(). The Material 3 colors are written first, so the receiver Style can override either:

val regular = GlassStyle.regular.material3()
val clear = GlassStyle.clear.material3(tint = Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.16f))

val custom = remember {
  GlassStyle { optics(GlassOptics.regular.copy(refractionStrength = 0.8f)) }
}
Modifier.hazeGlass(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = custom.material3(tint = Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.16f)),
)

Call it on GlassStyle for the Material 3 colors alone, for example as a subtree default:

CompositionLocalProvider(LocalGlassStyle provides GlassStyle.material3()) {
  // Glass modifiers in this subtree inherit the Material 3 surface background.
}

docs.title: Built-in styles
docs.text:
GlassStyle.regular is the default style. Its blur and depth grow with the surface's shortest side: compact controls keep some refracted detail and a curved edge, while larger surfaces fully diffuse the backdrop. In dark appearance it uses a darker tone, edge, and lighting response.

GlassStyle.clear keeps more of the background visible. It uses the same shallow blur at every size, with refraction concentrated in a band along the edge that forms loops around the corners. Fallback renderers keep Clear's background color, tint, and edges, but drop the refraction, blur, and tone adjustments that give it its look.

Prefer Regular when background content could interfere with labels or controls, especially for surfaces containing substantial text. Use Clear for controls over photos and video where the underlying content should remain visible. This follows Apple's Materials guidance. For Clear over bright content, add a dark dimming layer behind the controls when needed for contrast. Haze does not add dimming automatically.

Both styles are informed by iOS 27 Liquid Glass, but Haze does not promise pixel parity with iOS. They follow the system appearance supplied by the Compose host, which may reflect an app or window override; an unknown appearance uses the light response. They do not follow the iOS appearance slider or adapt to the content beneath them, so check foreground contrast with your own content.

Modifier.hazeGlass(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = GlassStyle.clear.material3(tint = Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.12f)),
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• backgroundColor: Color composited behind captured content before refraction and blur (defaults to transparent). Use an opaque color when transparent captured content must fully obscure the original sharp source.
  • tint: Glass tint (defaults to transparent).
  • optics: Optical configuration. See Choosing optics.
  • refractionDetailIntensity: Secondary edge-refraction detail strength 0..1. 0 disables it. GlassOptics defaults to 0.76; Regular uses 0, and Clear uses 0.76. Non-zero values add rendering work on full renderers.
  • specularIntensity: Highlight strength 0..1 (default 0.48).
  • edgeShadow: Shape-following dark rim beneath the specular highlight (defaults to black at 14% opacity). Its alpha controls strength; set Color.Transparent to disable it.
  • ambientResponse: Fresnel/edge lift 0..1 (default 0.15).
  • edgeSoftness: Soft fade at the edges (default 1.dp). Set to 0.dp for hard edges.
  • shape (RoundedCornerShape): Boundary for refraction and masking (default 16.dp corners). Add an outer Modifier.clip() with the same shape only when child content also needs clipping.
  • surfaceProfile: Cross-section for lighting and, with RefractionProfile.Surface, refraction. Options: Circle (default), Squircle, Lip, Concave.
  • lightPosition: Alignment of the light within the surface (default Alignment.Center). Start and end follow layout direction.
  • chromaticAberrationStrength: Dispersion strength 0..1 (default 0). Higher values produce prismatic color splitting at edges.
  • chromaticAberrationMode: Simple (default, cheaper) or Full (spectral, more expensive).
  • alpha: Overall opacity multiplier 0..1 (default 1). Values outside that range are clamped.

docs.title: Color handling
docs.text: chromaMultiplier values above 1f boost saturation without clipping colors that are already in the sRGB gamut; out-of-gamut source colors are left unchanged. tint and edgeShadow keep their Compose ColorSpace.

docs.title: GlassStyle
docs.text:
GlassStyle is safe to share. Build a base Style and use then for variations:

val baseStyle = GlassStyle {
  backgroundColor(Color.White)
  tint(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.16f))
  optics(GlassOptics.regular.copy(refractionStrength = 0.8f))
  shape(RoundedCornerShape(20.dp))
}
val emphasizedStyle = baseStyle.then { specularIntensity(0.7f) }

CompositionLocalProvider(LocalGlassStyle provides baseStyle) {
  // Use baseStyle as the default for Glass in this subtree.
}

A Style's block runs whenever a Glass surface resolves its style, not when the Style is built. The block may read snapshot state, such as an animated value; changes apply on the next frame without recomposing the hazeGlass call site. Keep the block free of side effects. Styles compare by identity, so remember or hoist a Style: a new Style in each composition replaces it on every surface.

val radius = animateDpAsState(if (expanded) 20.dp else 28.dp)
val style = remember {
  GlassStyle.regular.then { shape(RoundedCornerShape(radius.value)) }
}

Invalid values in a block throw IllegalArgumentException when the block runs, not where the Style is built; a GlassOptics value is validated when it is created. Values that animation can overshoot are coerced instead: alpha and tint alpha are clamped into 0f..1f, and negative corner radii are treated as zero. Validate or clamp other values from user input and remote data. Percent corner sizes, such as CircleShape, follow size changes without any state in the Style.

Each surface applies LocalGlassStyle and then its explicit Style. Values that neither sets come from Regular and GlassDefaults.

docs.title: Accessibility preferences
docs.text:
Haze does not read platform accessibility settings. Map them to GlassAccessibilitySettings and provide it where Glass is used:

CompositionLocalProvider(
  LocalGlassAccessibilitySettings provides GlassAccessibilitySettings(
    reduceTransparency = reduceTransparency,
    increaseContrast = increaseContrast,
    showBorders = showBorders,
  ),
) {
  // Glass here diffuses the background more or strengthens its separating edge when requested.
}

The defaults leave the Style unchanged, and the settings never modify your Style values. reduceTransparency uses a stronger, fully diffused blur during full rendering. In fallback rendering, it hides source detail with an opaque base: white in light appearance (also the default when appearance is unknown), or black in dark appearance. Light or dark comes from the system appearance that the Compose host supplies: LocalConfiguration.uiMode on Android, where anything other than night mode is light, and LocalSystemTheme on other platforms. An app or window override of those values is followed. MaterialTheme and other in-app theme state are not read. Set reducedTransparencyFallbackColor to an opaque Color to override this base, for example when your app has its own light and dark setting; null selects the automatic colour. Translucent and unspecified overrides are rejected.

Fallback draws this base, then your background colour, then tint. Overall alpha still fades the whole material, so source detail is hidden at alpha 1 and can show through during a fade. Turning reduceTransparency off restores ordinary fallback rendering. The colour override only affects reduced-transparency fallback; full rendering keeps its stronger blur.

increaseContrast raises tone contrast and enforces a visible edge. showBorders enforces a visible edge without changing tone. The edge appears even when the Style has zero edge softness.

docs.title: Light alignment
docs.text:
Use Compose Alignment values so lighting adapts to each surface. Logical alignments such as Alignment.CenterStart and Alignment.CenterEnd also follow LTR or RTL layout direction.

val sharedLighting = GlassStyle {
  lightPosition(Alignment.CenterStart)
}

Use BiasAlignment for a continuous proportional position:

val movingLighting = GlassStyle {
  lightPosition(BiasAlignment(horizontalBias = 0.4f, verticalBias = -0.6f))
}

docs.title: Style defaults
docs.text:
hazeGlass uses GlassStyle.regular when you omit style. Use LocalGlassStyle to set a default for a subtree, and pass an explicit Style when one element needs to differ.

Box(
  Modifier
    .size(180.dp)
    .hazeGlass(input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState)),
)

docs.title: Choosing optics
docs.text:
Use GlassStyle.regular for the built-in material:

val regular = GlassStyle.regular

For direct optical control, call optics(...) in a custom Style. The GlassOptics constructor defaults are not Regular's. For example, the constructor defaults to a 15.dp refraction displacement and RefractionProfile.Surface, while Regular uses 48.dp and Edge(20.dp). To change part of the built-in material, start from GlassOptics.regular.copy(...):

GlassStyle {
  optics(
    GlassOptics.regular.copy(
      blurRadius = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(20.dp),
      refractionStrength = 0.8f,
      refractionHeightFraction = 0.3f,
      refractionDisplacement = 18.dp,
      refractionFoldStrength = 0.65f,
      depth = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(0.5f),
    ),
  )
}

Use optics { copy(...) } to adjust the optical configuration established by earlier style writes:

val softerClear = GlassStyle.clear.then {
  optics { copy(blurRadius = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(4.dp)) }
}

The receiver starts from GlassOptics.regular and then includes optics from LocalGlassStyle and earlier writes in the Style, including built-in Styles it extends. The block runs on every style evaluation and can read snapshot state without recomposing the call site. Keep it free of side effects. Later optics(value) writes or built-in styles replace its result.

For a configuration you want to store or choose outside a style, copy GlassOptics.regular or GlassOptics.clear:

val softerClearOptics = GlassOptics.clear.copy(blurRadius = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(4.dp))
val softerClear = GlassStyle.clear.then { optics(softerClearOptics) }

optics(value) replaces the whole optical model. To vary blur or depth with size, give GlassOptics points keyed by the surface's shortest side. Values hold at the end points and blend smoothly between them. Each responsive value needs at least two points with positive, finite, strictly increasing sizes:

val responsiveOptics = GlassOptics.regular.copy(
  blurRadius = OpticalSizeValue.Responsive(
    OpticalSizePoint(176.dp, 8.dp),
    OpticalSizePoint(300.dp, 12.dp),
  ),
  depth = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(0.4f),
)
val style = GlassStyle { optics(responsiveOptics) }

Keep a GlassOptics value when it is reused, stored, copied, or selected programmatically:

val reusableOptics = GlassOptics.regular.copy(
  blurRadius = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(20.dp),
)
val style = GlassStyle { optics(reusableOptics) }

Optics also accept a progressive intensity:

GlassStyle {
  tint(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.20f))
  optics(
    GlassOptics.regular.copy(
      progressive = HazeProgressive.verticalGradient(
        startIntensity = 1f,
        endIntensity = 0.25f,
      ),
    ),
  )
}

refractionProfile chooses where refraction happens:

  • RefractionProfile.Surface (the GlassOptics default) refracts across the surface, following surfaceProfile and refractionHeightFraction.
  • RefractionProfile.Edge(width) refracts most at the boundary and fades to none over width. Refraction follows wider corners than the visible shape, and displacement is capped at half the shortest side, so compact capsules refract less than large cards. refractionHeightFraction then affects lighting only. A zero width disables refraction.

Regular uses Edge(20.dp), strength 0.7, displacement 48.dp, and lighting height fraction 0.15. Clear uses Edge(28.dp), strength 0.85, displacement 56.dp, and lighting height fraction 0.35.

refractionFoldStrength (0f..1f, default 0f) folds refraction back on itself near the edge. It works with every SurfaceProfile and stays within refractionDisplacement.

GlassOptics controls appearance; HazePerformanceMode controls the quality and cost trade-off.

docs.title: Retained output
docs.text:
When all of its sources disappear, Glass keeps drawing its last output by default (HazeSourceRetention.KeepLastFrame). This keeps source transitions smooth, but can briefly show pixels from removed content.

This is not a frozen copy of the last frame. On Android, retained Glass can redraw from a source's current pixels when it becomes visible again, and content changed inside a source after capture can appear. For privacy-sensitive content, use ClearWhenUnavailable:

Modifier.hazeGlass(
  input = HazeInput.Sources(
    state = hazeState,
    retention = HazeSourceRetention.ClearWhenUnavailable,
  ),
)

docs.title: Android window-backdrop Glass
docs.text:
HazeInput.Backdrop samples the pixels already drawn earlier in the current window. On Android its native path is experimental; enable it before the Glass surface attaches:

HazeFeatureFlags.isPlatformBackdropEnabled = true

Modifier.hazeGlass(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = GlassStyle.regular,
)

Native Glass keeps the full look, including refraction, blur, chromatic aberration, rim lighting, and interaction lighting. It cannot select a Haze source, include content drawn later, or cross a dialog, popup, or window boundary.

The flag makes Glass eligible, not guaranteed. Where native rendering is unavailable or fails, HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState) renders from its source fallback, while HazeInput.Backdrop(), which has no fallback, draws its content without Glass. A frame that native rendering cannot handle after it has started also draws content without Glass for that frame. Changing the flag affects later attachments only. See Android window backdrops for eligibility, fallback, and diagnostics.

Use HazeInput.Sources directly when exact source selection, cross-window alignment, or retained output must govern the actual input rather than only the fallback.

docs.title: Fallbacks
docs.text:
Use one GlassStyle on every platform. Haze chooses the available renderer automatically, so you don't need capability checks or a second Style.

Fallback rendering keeps the material recognizable but simplifies advanced optics:

Authored behavior Preferred rendering Fallback Tint, alpha, and rounded shape Preserved Preserved Ambient edge response and edge softness Preserved Approximated as a soft rim Specular intensity and resolved light Alignment Preserved Approximated as an aligned radial highlight Interaction lighting and transforms Preserved Preserved Fixed or responsive refraction, blur, and progressive optics Preserved Omitted Chromatic aberration, surface profile, and advanced color adjustments Preserved Omitted Interaction refraction and white-point deltas Preserved Omitted Glass container clusters Members merge into one shape with smooth bridges One surface per cluster, clipped to the hard union of the member shapes, with no bridge

Don't make essential meaning depend on refraction or chromatic aberration alone, because fallback rendering omits them.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Start with HazePerformanceMode.Default (the fixed Balanced profile) and tune only after measuring a representative screen. The performance guide explains which Glass-specific workloads and interactions to test.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
Glass interaction is opt-in. It adds a visual response only: no click handling, focusability, semantics, or keyboard/D-pad activation.

Modifier.hazeGlass(
  input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
  style = GlassStyle {
    pressed {
      lightingIntensity(1f)
      refractionMultiplier(1.08f)
      whitePointDelta(0.04f)
      scale(0.98f)
    }
  },
)

Declare only the states and responses you need. For focus and keyboard/D-pad activation, share one remembered MutableInteractionSource between the Glass modifier and your behavior modifiers:

val interactionStyle = GlassStyle {
  hovered { lightingIntensity(0.35f) }
  focused { lightingIntensity(0.35f) }
  pressed {
    lightingIntensity(1f)
    refractionMultiplier(1.08f)
    whitePointDelta(0.04f)
    scale(0.98f)
  }
  interactionLightRadiusFraction(0.7f)
  interactionPositionAnimationSpec(
    spring(dampingRatio = 1f, stiffness = Spring.StiffnessMedium),
  )
}

val interactionSource = remember { MutableInteractionSource() }

Modifier
  .clickable(interactionSource = interactionSource, indication = null) { onClick() }
  .focusable(interactionSource = interactionSource)
  .hazeGlass(
    input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
    style = interactionStyle,
    interactionSource = interactionSource,
    interactionTransformTarget = GlassTransformTarget.MaterialAndContent,
    interactionTransformPivot = GlassTransformPivot.Pointer,
    interactionReducedMotionPolicy = GlassReducedMotionPolicy.System,
  )

The visual response lives in GlassStyle; the interaction source and behavior options are passed per element to hazeGlass, so one Style can be reused without sharing interaction state.

Mouse, stylus, and touch positions are tracked immediately. interactionPositionAnimationSpec animates the light towards focus and other InteractionSource-derived positions.

When states overlap, pressed takes priority over hovered, which takes priority over focused. Use animate(toSpec, fromSpec) when arrival and departure need different motion.

GlassStyle {
  pressed {
    animate(
      toSpec = spring(dampingRatio = 0.82f, stiffness = Spring.StiffnessMedium),
      fromSpec = spring(
        dampingRatio = 0.72f,
        stiffness = Spring.StiffnessMediumLow,
      ),
    ) {
      scale(0.98f)
    }
  }
}
  • interactionTransformTarget transforms the material only, or the material and its content.
  • interactionTransformPivot scales around the Pointer or the Center.
  • interactionReducedMotionPolicy: System follows the system animation scale and behaves as Reduced when that scale is zero, Reduced snaps lighting and optics and suppresses transforms, and Full always animates.

Omit a state block from a replacement Style to remove that response.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Wrap nearby Glass surfaces in Modifier.hazeGlassContainer to merge them into one shape, for controls that should read as one object, such as a toolbar or a segmented control. See Glass containers for the merge rule, transitions, lazy layouts and fallbacks.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Box(
  Modifier
    .size(180.dp)
    .hazeGlass(
      input = HazeInput.Backdrop(hazeState),
      style = GlassStyle {
        tint(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.16f))
        optics(
          GlassOptics.regular.copy(
            refractionStrength = 0.8f,
            refractionHeightFraction = 0.32f,
            depth = OpticalSizeValue.Fixed(0.5f),
          ),
        )
        specularIntensity(0.7f)
        ambientResponse(0.7f)
        edgeSoftness(14.dp)
        shape(RoundedCornerShape(20.dp))
        surfaceProfile(SurfaceProfile.Squircle)
        chromaticAberrationStrength(0.2f)
      },
    )
)

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep chromaticAberrationStrength modest; start at 0.1-0.25 to avoid rainbow artifacts.
  • Combine edgeSoftness with rounded shapes for smooth clipping; set edgeSoftness = 0.dp to rely purely on the shape.
  • Use SurfaceProfile.Concave for an inward-curving bezel or SurfaceProfile.Lip for a raised rim effect.

docs.title: Glass containers
docs.text:
A Glass container draws its Glass members' surfaces together, so that nearby members merge into one shape. Use it for controls that should read as one object, such as a toolbar or a segmented control, and for surfaces that appear next to an existing one and should grow out of it.

This page assumes you are familiar with Glass styles, inputs and interaction.

docs.title: Container and members
docs.text:
// Styles compare by identity, so remember the style.
val style = remember { GlassStyle.regular.then { shape(CircleShape) } }

Row(
  modifier = Modifier.hazeGlassContainer(spacing = 16.dp),
  horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(4.dp),
) {
  repeat(3) {
    Box(
      Modifier
        .size(48.dp)
        .hazeGlass(input = HazeInput.Sources(hazeState), style = style),
    )
  }
}

spacing is required, finite and not negative. A spacing of zero disables bridges. Optionally pass transitionSpec and reducedMotionPolicy, which are described under Transitions.

Every hazeGlass modifier below the container becomes a member of its nearest container. A member keeps its own style, shape, colors and interaction response. A hazeGlass modifier outside a container is unchanged.

docs.title: Merge rule
docs.text:
Members join a cluster when the gap between them is less than half of the spacing. The container draws each cluster as one surface, with smooth bridges between the members. A member that joins no cluster draws as a separate surface.

Members merge only when all of these hold:

  • Same input and rendering options. Equal input (for HazeInput.Sources, the same hazeState, selection and retention), performance mode and expandLayerBounds.
  • Same material. Equal optics, surface profile, specular and edge settings, chromatic aberration, tone, light position and alpha. Regular and Clear surfaces therefore never merge. Shape, tint, background color and interaction responses may differ; colors blend across the bridge.
  • No rotation or scale. A member rotated or scaled by its layout, for example with graphicsLayer, draws separately. Translation and a layer alpha, such as an AnimatedVisibility fade, don't prevent merging.
  • Adjacent in order. Members are ordered by when they attach: composition order at first, with members added later placed after the existing ones. Only members next to each other in that order share a cluster. A non-matching member between two compatible ones splits them, even when it is far away, because merging never changes drawing order.
  • At most four per cluster. Extra members draw separately, without a bridge. Where an extra member overlaps the cluster, blur and tint apply twice in the overlap.

Lower-quality performance modes also render the merged shape at lower resolution.

docs.title: Optical size
docs.text:
A container uses one optical size: the largest shortest side among its members. Every member's optics use that size, whether or not it is in a cluster, so a small member next to a large one takes on the large member's diffusion, even when the two don't merge.

The size updates immediately, without animation, when a member is added, removed or resized. Members that are animating out, or whose bounds have collapsed to zero area, don't count.

docs.title: Where Glass samples from
docs.text: A container draws all of its members' Glass behind all of its children. With HazeInput.Backdrop, the glass samples only content drawn before the container. With HazeInput.Sources, the glass samples the captured sources as usual. Joining or leaving a cluster never changes a member's z-order.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text: Interaction responses work as described in Glass interaction, applied to the member's own part of the merged shape: pressing a member scales and lights only that part. A uniform pressed scale does not split the cluster.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
A member that attaches or detaches after the container's first draw animates its glass. Choose the transition with hazeGlass(memberTransition = ...):

  • GlassMemberTransition.MatchedGeometry is the default. A member that attaches within the spacing of another member grows out of it, and a member that detaches retracts into it. Beyond the spacing, it falls back to Materialize.
  • GlassMemberTransition.Materialize fades the glass in or out where it is. A fading member draws on its own until it is fully opaque.
  • GlassMemberTransition.None applies no transition.

transitionSpec times the animation and defaults to spring(). Members with GlassMemberTransition.None do not animate. reducedMotionPolicy decides how the transition responds to the platform motion-duration scale:

  • GlassReducedMotionPolicy.System, the default, follows the scale. Above zero, transitions run under that scale. At zero, because animations are off, members snap: they appear and disappear with no transition, as with GlassMemberTransition.None.
  • GlassReducedMotionPolicy.Reduced keeps the morph but uses a critically damped spring, so it does not overshoot, at full duration whatever the scale is. The spring keeps transitionSpec's stiffness when it is a spring and otherwise uses medium stiffness.
  • GlassReducedMotionPolicy.Full uses transitionSpec as written, whatever the scale is.

Changes to transitionSpec and reducedMotionPolicy apply from the next transition.

Haze animates only the glass. Animate member content yourself, for example with AnimatedVisibility and fades. Don't animate a member's layout scale: a scaled member stops merging and loses its matched-geometry transition.

The glass disappears immediately, without a transition, when:

  • the member uses HazeInput.Content;
  • the member is rotated or scaled;
  • no remaining member uses the same input and sources, including when the last member leaves.

A member whose nearest container changes while it stays in the layout, for example when a nested container is added or removed around it, appears in the new container immediately. Moving a member with movableContentOf detaches and reattaches it, so it detaches from the old container and attaches to the new one, each with the transition described above. A running transition ends without animating when the member it grows from or retracts into leaves, or moves beyond the spacing.

docs.title: Lazy layouts
docs.text:
Pass the lazy layout's state to hazeGlassContainer as scrollState. While that state is scrolling, including the frame in which it stops, members appear and disappear without a transition, whatever their memberTransition. Items inserted or removed while the layout is idle still animate, but a scroll that starts while an item's glass is still animating out ends that animation immediately.

// Styles compare by identity, so remember the style.
val style = remember { GlassStyle.regular.then { shape(CircleShape) } }
val listState = rememberLazyListState()

LazyRow(
  state = listState,
  modifier = Modifier.hazeGlassContainer(spacing = 16.dp, scrollState = listState),
  horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),
) {
  items(chips, key = { it.id }) { chip ->
    Chip(
      chip = chip,
      modifier = Modifier.hazeGlass(
        input = HazeInput.Sources(hazeState),
        style = style,
      ),
    )
  }
}

Drags, flings, animateScrollBy and scrollToItem are scrolls. Position changes made outside a scroll, such as requestScrollToItem or dispatchRawDelta, are not, so their items animate.

Without scrollState, items that scroll into view animate like any other new member. With the default MatchedGeometry, an item's glass grows out of its neighbor and lags its content, and an item that scrolls out leaves a trailing ghost until the animation ends. Items present at the container's first draw never animate.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text:
Without RuntimeShader support, or when a cluster is too large to render in full, each cluster draws as one surface clipped to the hard union of the member shapes, with no bridge. Members keep their own tint and background color; where members overlap, the earlier member's colors apply. Each member resolves GlassAccessibilitySettings and appearance in its own context. With reduceTransparency, it draws an opaque white/light or black/dark base (or its opaque reducedTransparencyFallbackColor override), then its authored background colour and tint. Earlier members still own overlapping regions, and overall alpha still fades the material. Disabling the preference restores that member's ordinary fallback appearance.

Per-member press lighting is still drawn. See Fallbacks for what else fallback rendering omits.

docs.title: Samples
docs.text:
